question: Our office relocation looked straightforward on paper, yet each step turned into a slog: a late truck, a missing key, rain, a nervous crew. Is there a name for that drag that turns plain jobs hard?
text:
That phenomenon is known as friction[1].
The concept was famously defined by military theorist Carl von Clausewitz, who observed that "everything in war is simple, but the simplest thing is difficult"[2]. He described friction as "the force that makes the apparently easy so difficult"—an unseen drag that resists all action, saps energy, and turns straightforward jobs into an exhausting slog[1].
Friction is rarely caused by a single major catastrophe; instead, it is the accumulation of minor, unexpected obstacles[1][2]. The doctrine in your sources breaks friction down into several categories that map directly onto your relocation experience[3]:
Physical and External Friction: Uncontrollable environmental or logistical factors, such as bad weather or rain[3].
Mental and Psychological Friction: Human factors like stress, hesitation, or a nervous crew[3].
Self-Induced Friction: Internal operational snags, such as a late truck, a missing key, or gaps in coordination[3].
While the term originated in military strategy, it is widely used across organizational management and systems theory to explain why plans that look simple on paper routinely run into real-world resistance[1][3].

Portrayed as a clash between two opposing wills, war appears a simple enterprise. In practice, the conduct of war becomes extremely difficult because of the countless factors that impinge on it. These factors collectively have been called friction, which Clausewitz described as "the force that makes the apparently easy so difficult."5 Friction is the force that resists all action and saps energy. It makes the simple difficult and the difficult seemingly impossible.

The very essence of war as a clash between opposed wills creates friction. In this dynamic environment of interacting forces, friction abounds.
Friction may be mental, as in indecision over a course of action. It may be physical, as in effective enemy fire or a terrain obstacle that must be overcome. Friction may be external, imposed by enemy action, the terrain, weather, or mere chance. Friction may be self-induced, caused by such factors
